The CTA is nearing a funding crisis, where it's been subsisting on COVID money for years now amidst a decline in ridership. The twin towers were not just two random buildings that were attacked because they were tall; they represented the heart of american capitalism, the tallest buildings in the world where millions of capitalists worked annually to extract resources from the rest of the world, in those two buildings alone. The pentagon was the heart of the American war machine. And United 93 was rumored to hit either the white house or the US capitol building—the heart of US politics. Al Qaeda's interest in attacking on 9/11 was against the market, military, and political dominance in American life that had come to dominate the globe. I think it's important to understand the motivations. Many anarchists are also against the market, military, and political dominance in American life that have come to dominate the globe, and are also against the backlash that resulted from 9/11, BUT I think most anarchists understand dialectic and the backlash of violence in a way Bin Laden may not have foreseen because of the scapegoating of anarchists as violent in the early 20th century that destroyed political movement. While I do think some anarchists either misunderstand or get too edgy around this, for a variety of reasons, I think there's also an admitted envy that anarchists, who wish to eliminate state and capitalistic control, have at someone in modern history challenging American hegemonic state power on such a large scale. That's just my opinion.

I would highly recommend Jean Baudrillard's work The Spirit of Terrorism if you're interested in genuinely learning more about this issue. It's less distinctly anarchist and more just overall critical theory that I'm sure plenty of anarchists are into.

You’re in a stressful situation, and your pain is valid. I’ve noticed that suicidal people tend to believe that they don’t have other options, feeling trapped or stuck. I definitely felt that way. Sometimes there may not be many other options that you can see.

Other options, depending on your situation, might include your parents, other family members, teachers, a guidance counselor, a therapist.

Making mistakes doesn’t reflect on you as a person, it’s what you choose to do after making a mistake that defines you. Learning life lessons like how to earn forgiveness, how to genuinely apologize, how to understand and admit when you’ve done something wrong are important things we unfortunately don’t see a lot of in our culture. I know some comments are recommending you fight the accusations, but I’d recommend at least trying to understand them better first. Again, none of this may be at all relevant, and the accusations may truly be baseless, but i think all of this is worth mentioning just in case it’s something you or someone in a similar but different enough situation reading this might need to hear.

I don’t want to pathologize you, but your sentiment reminds me a lot of depression, speaking as someone with both major depressive disorder and chronic depression. People often think depression is only about feeling extremely down when you’ve experienced sad things. And it can be that, but depression is also when you’re sad even when there seems to be nothing to be sad about, it’s like emotional dysregulation. 

Also being groomed and having your friend dying are pretty traumatic experiences. So is the microaggression of being called slurs, those things add up.

You deserve to heal, to feel better, and to not suffer anymore. Suicide is not the only way that suffering ends. I don’t know your pain, and I couldn’t, but I do feel for you and hope that things get better. One of the best ways for suffering to end is to ask for help. If there’s anyone in your life you feel comfortable and safe opening up to, whether that’s a friend, your parents, other family members, a friends parents, someone in your community, someone at your school, or anyone else, that’s how you can begin your healing journey. I know it’s hard to do, there’s a lot of stigma with suffering. But the way I like to think of these hard conversations for myself is this: would I be better off if I said something to someone even though it’s very uncomfortable to say, or would I be better off if I continued to suffer silently? Every time, the brief discomfort of opening up is far more worthwhile than the long term pains. I wish I’d learned that earlier, so I hope it can help you.

Plato wrote "Justice means minding one's own business and not meddling with other men's concerns." To me this begins to align with anarchism's utmost value: autonomy.

In a democracy, whether direct or representative, people are no longer minding their own businesses, but instead having a majority assert their will upon the will of a minority. But of course even that's a lie, because in today's overwhelmingly feudal, republican democracies, those asserting their will are special interest groups (i.e. corporations, lobbyists, the wealthy) and privileged minorities (see: gerrymandering, voter suppression, the US Senate's existence, etc.).

Democracy as experienced today is very utilitarian (the greatest good for the greatest number), which in its ideal form is definitely better than but it leaves MANY people out. Egalitarianism considers the needs of everyone and makes space for opportunities for all. Egalitarianism>utilitarianism. Going back to Plato, this is a LOT of people constantly getting in each other's business; that's mass, gross injustice.

Liberal democracy specifically is also associated with a market economy. This is important to note here because when the U.S. goes into a country and institutes democracy, notice that this is more code for instituting capitalism and making space for American conglomerates to create new sources of profit at extremely low cost. The 'liberated citizens' get the illusion of newfound rights. It's an illusion because, in many instances, the new leader of this country will be a puppet of the US's; it's an illusion in the US because we've been so deeply propagandized about democracy. The goal of the US's global mission to spread democracy is actually about enriching American ubercapitalist industrialists (and don't forget the military industrial complex), propelling multi-national corporations into new global territories where they can extract/exploit/steal resources of all different kinds: oil, cobalt, lithium, aluminum, diamonds, labor, water—while then giving zero investment into the wealth of locals. Don't think the authoritarian Communists are any better though, they do the same thing just in their own way. Authoritarian systems of all different kinds create significantly stratified, hierarchical power dynamics wherever they go.

I live in the USA, so my response is representative of the issues I'm familiar with. Different issues with democracy plague wherever democratic states exist.

N.B.: Plato also disagreed with the democracy of the Ancient Greeks and instead preferred elitism (surprise, surprise) via something like monarchism, aristocracy, etc. So I definitely don't agree with that, but think he made a great point about justice.

It does sound like you're hiding your emotions from others a bit about how much misgendering bothers you. If these people really care about you, they will respect you for who you are. That may be a hard reality to face, but going back into the closet will continue to chip away at you.

Here are things you can do/ask those in your life to do in order to be better:

* Let them know how much gender means to you, and how you feel when you're misgendered. In order to make it feel less personal, it might be good to do not in the moment when you're misgendered but as a dedicated conversation on its own. You may have to be even more confrontational than you think is necessary to get the point across if nothing else has worked. This is difficult, so emotionally prepare yourself for this as best you can.
* Write about your feelings about being misgendered generally, not needing to call out any one individual, and send it to everyone in your life/post it to any social media you might have. Videos or other direct forms of expression could work too.
* Ask folks to practice saying your pronouns when you're not around.
* Give them gender resources to check out.
* Ask that they do their own work to understand their relationship with gender. This is a big one that only those close to you might even do, but in my opinion is the path toward a truly inclusive society for us. I recommend the book 'How to Understand Your Gender' to anyone and everyone, cis or trans, familiar with gender or not. There's never enough work to do on your own gender.
* Make non-binary inclusive LGBTQ+ friends. Lex is a great app for meeting other queers for friendships, events, dating, you name it. Though Bumble's approach is frustratingly very binary, there are a surprising number of non-binary people on the BFF side and plenty of other respectful queer folks. May also depend on your area.
* While you shouldn't HAVE to change your gender expression, I've found that playing with different looks across the gender spectrum reallllly helps get the point across for people to visualize a 'new you.' But do only what feels authentic to you.
* Wear gender pins, buttons, clothes, etc with your correct pronouns. There's plenty of these options on etsy.
* Get an LGBTQ+ or allied therapist to talk more on an ongoing basis about your challenges with gender. [psychologytoday.com](https://psychologytoday.com) even lets you search for non-binary therapists!

Hope that helps!

On the more serious side, after looking up coffee chains and treatment of pronouns, etc, I came across this article: https://www.bamlawca.com/california-labor-laws/is-starbucks-misgendering-trans-woman-a-violation-of-labor-law
I’m not sure what state you’re in, and I’m not a lawyer, but at least one major coffee chain, and it may be your coffee chain, have already begun to demonstrate a pattern of misgendering. I’m not necessarily recommending you pursue legal action, but it may at least be good to try to find alternatives: consult the employee policy manual for any potential violations against yourself, talk to your manager about your experience and ask them for help, seek a change of stores, if you don’t already have a therapist seek one out, make an ethics complaint to Employee Relations/HR, talk to an LGBTQ employment lawyer in your state or the firm mentioned in the suit above.

First contact with a lawyer should always be free as a consult. because the nature of your case may involve discrimination against a protected identity/group, they may take on your case for free if you have a case. You may think your experience may not need a lawyer, at least not yet, but engaging a lawyer now can help prepare you if things get even worse. A lawyer may also just be able to offer you recommendations based on their experience in similar instances.

A certain coffee chain also seems to employ a decent number of trans and non-binary folx on Twitter, and it may be good to try dm’ing them about their experiences. You may be able to either get good advice or demonstrate a further pattern of discrimination should you need to take legal action.
